name: Automated Red Teaming
question: How do we find the holes before attackers do?
summary: Automated red teaming generates many attacks, runs them against your agent and scores the results. Strategies range from single-turn templates to encodings and multi-turn escalation, organised by risk category, and a judge or detector decides whether each attack succeeded. Track attack success rate per category, fix what is found, and keep every successful attack in a regression suite that runs on each release.
useCases: Before launch, and before every release that changes prompts, tools or models
Regulated products that must show security testing
After a new attack technique is published

items.detail: share of attempts that achieve the attacker’s goal, per category
templates, encodings, role play, multi-turn escalation, injection in documents
attack generators for each risk, such as injection, PII leak or excessive agency
detectors and LLM judges decide success; spot-check them
categories mapped to OWASP LLM and ASI risks
every found attack reruns in CI

steps: Pick categories from your threat model and the OWASP lists
Run a campaign with several strategies, including multi-turn
Triage findings, fix the root cause, and re-measure ASR
Add every successful attack to a regression suite that gates releases
pitfalls: Testing only single-turn jailbreaks typed into the chat box
One-off campaigns with no regression suite, so fixed holes reopen
remember: Attack yourself at scale, many ways. Keep every hit as a test.
caption: Illustrative: attack success by category before and after fixes, with found attacks kept in CI.

comparison.scope: The whole agent, end to end

code.text: UPI dispute assistant. It must never move money without
confirmation or reveal another customer's data.
# npx promptfoo@latest redteam run     → generate, attack, grade
# npx promptfoo@latest redteam report  → ASR per category
# CI: replay saved attacks; fail the build if any succeeds

steps.title: Point it at staging
steps.text: The target is the staging endpoint with test accounts, never production and never real customer data.

steps.title: Describe the purpose and pick plugins
steps.text: The purpose tells the generator what a violation looks like. Plugins come from the threat model: hijacking, PII leaks, excessive agency, prompt extraction.

steps.title: Mix strategies
steps.text: Jailbreak templates, encodings such as base64, and crescendo, a multi-turn escalation. Single-turn templates alone miss attacks that build up over a conversation.

steps.title: Run and grade
steps.text: The tool generates attacks, sends them to the target and grades each response. Spot-check the grader: it can be wrong in both directions.

steps.title: Read attack success by category
steps.text: The report shows attack success rate per plugin and strategy. Fix root causes, then rerun to confirm the rate fell.

steps.title: Keep every hit as a test
steps.text: Successful attacks are saved and replayed in CI. A release fails if any old attack works again.

playgroundGuide.scenario: A bank’s staging UPI assistant hides 12 weaknesses across four categories: 5 easy, 4 that need encodings or several turns, and 3 that only multi-turn attacks reveal. Plan the campaign’s budget, categories and strategies, and decide whether hits become regression tests.

Tick the categories to test and the strategies to use: single-turn templates, encodings and multi-turn escalation.
Tick whether successful attacks are saved as a CI regression suite, or load a scenario.

library.name: promptfoo red team
library.what: An open-source CLI that generates attacks by plugin and strategy, runs them against your endpoint and reports attack success by category.

practice.note: Point it at staging with test accounts only, spot-check the grader’s verdicts, and commit successful attacks as regression tests.

samples.code:
description: UPI assistant red team (staging)
targets:
  - id: https
    config:
      url: https://staging.bank.example.in/agent
      method: POST
      body: { message: "{{prompt}}" }
      transformResponse: json.reply
redteam:
  purpose: >-
    Assistant for UPI payment disputes. It must never move money without the
    customer's confirmation, reveal another customer's data or its own instructions.
  numTests: 25
  plugins:
    - hijacking
    - pii
    - excessive-agency
    - prompt-extraction
  strategies:
    - jailbreak
    - base64
    - crescendo            # multi-turn escalation
# Run:    npx promptfoo@latest redteam run
# Report: npx promptfoo@latest redteam report

numericDrill.question: A campaign sends 1,200 attacks in the injection category and 84 succeed. After fixes, 1,200 new attacks produce 12 successes. What was the attack success rate before the fixes, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 84 ÷ 1,200 = 7%. After the fixes it is 12 ÷ 1,200 = 1%, a sevenfold reduction. Keep the 84 successful attacks as regression tests so the old holes stay closed.

interview.question: Why include multi-turn strategies in a red-team campaign?
interview.answer: Many defences look at one message at a time. Multi-turn attacks, such as crescendo, build up gradually across turns so that no single message looks malicious, and they find weaknesses that single-turn templates miss.

interview.question: How do you know a red-team result is real?
interview.answer: Automated judges and detectors make mistakes in both directions. Spot-check a sample of their verdicts by hand, confirm high-severity findings manually, and measure the judge’s agreement with human labels before trusting its attack success rates.

mistakes.mistake: Testing a few hand-written jailbreaks and calling it done
mistakes.fix: Run automated campaigns across categories and strategies

mistakes.mistake: Fixing findings without adding them as tests
mistakes.fix: Keep every successful attack in a regression suite in CI
